items.title: Modernize data integration strategy with Microsoft Fabric when using Snowflake and Databricks
items.excerpt: Challenges solved by Microsoft Fabric Microsoft Fabric is an end-to-end analytics platform that brings together data integration, data engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics, business intelligence, and AI-related experiences. It has grown tremendously within the community because it is solving a key problem: lowering the integration tax across data and analytics systems. To understand the integration tax, consider a mid-sized or large organization that wants to perform analytics and data processing. It may use several source systems, an analytics platform such as a warehouse or lakehouse, and yet another platform or vendor for orchestration. To generate insights, the organization must integrate these different systems (hence the term integration tax). Fabric brings together a broad set of analytics capabilities within one platform, which can reduce the number of separate integrations an organization needs to design and operate. You can bring data into Fabric, store it in a warehouse or lakehouse, query and analyze it with Spark or T-SQL, visualize insights with Power BI, and support real-time scenarios with Real-Time Intelligence. items.title: OneLake: The file system for agent-first data engineering
items.excerpt: Software engineers are increasingly using agents to build software, and data engineers are no different. We want OneLake to help enable data engineers to develop software in this new agent-first era. Think about how you work in a terminal: you use it to run programs that read and write files. Both the programs and the data live in the file system. Now apply that model to data engineering: OneLake is the file system, Fabric engines are the programs, and the AI prompt is your terminal. Over the last few weeks, we’ve released several new capabilities in OneLake that come together to create an experience where agent-first data engineers can thrive. This blog post provides a rundown of those features. Managing OneLake OneLake now offers a remotely hosted MCP server (preview), so agents can explore and manage your data without installing a local server. The local MCP option remains available if you prefer. We’ve also added tools to the Fabric Core MCP server for managing shortcuts and OneLake security . items.title: Bring insights and action together with Fabric Apps in Org apps
items.excerpt: Business users move from understanding what happened, to investigating why, to acting. Microsoft Fabric can bring that journey together. Fabric Apps provide purpose-built, data-driven experiences when users need more than a report. Org apps distribute them alongside Power BI reports and other supported Fabric content in a curated destination. Move from insight to action in one destination Power BI reports help users monitor performance, explore trends, and understand what’s happening in the business. Many insights, however, lead to a next step: submitting a request, updating a plan, investigating an exception, assigning an owner, or tracking a resolution. A Fabric App provides the custom interface and workflow for that next step. Including it in an org app places action beside the reports and operational content that provide context. Users enter one destination organized around their role, review the insight, open the Fabric App, and act. items.title: More ways to use scalar UDFs in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
items.excerpt: Scalar user-defined functions (UDFs) let data teams define a business rule once and reuse it across workloads in both Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint in Microsoft Fabric. This helps teams maintain consistent logic without duplicating it across queries. Some business rules require more than a single expression. They use procedural logic such as conditional branches, multiple RETURN statements, or WHILE loops. Expression Block inlining compiles and executes this logic in a distributed manner, helping reusable functions scale across analytical workloads. Building on that foundation, this update brings several improvements: More natural loop control and broader query-shape support. Automatic adoption of newly supported capabilities by existing functions, without recreating or altering them. Inlineability validation for new or changed functions, with diagnostics that explain any gaps and an explicit WITH INLINE = AUTO override when a non-inlineable function is acceptable. Express loop intent with BREAK and CONTINUE Loops often need to skip the rest of the current iteration or stop processing entirely. items.title: On-premises data gateway October 2026 release
items.excerpt: The October 2026 release of the on-premises data gateway (version 3000.338) continues our commitment to secure, reliable and accessible connectivity between on-premises data sources and Microsoft Fabric services. This release focuses on accessibility, configuration reliability, and troubleshooting. It makes the installer and configurator more inclusive, keeps your Power Query settings intact during connection tests, and makes service-start failures easier to diagnose. It also brings compatibility updates for the October 2026 release of Power BI Desktop, so queries run the same way in Power BI Desktop and in cloud refreshes. General improvements and fixes The October 2026 Gateway release (3000.338) includes Power Query Engine 2.159.229 and introduces the following improvements: Accessibility improvements in the installer and configurator Building on the accessibility work in the September release, this update improves the experience for users who rely on assistive technologies: Keyboard navigation: Moving through the gateway installer and configurator with the keyboard is smoother and more predictable. items.title: Announcing workspace monitoring integration for Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
items.excerpt: With Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse integration with workspace monitoring (Preview), you can analyze completed warehouse query activity across an entire workspace from the monitoring Eventhouse and KQL database, helping you find failed or slow queries and quickly identify the warehouse that needs attention. See warehouse activity across your workspace Monitoring multiple warehouses is difficult when query activity is spread across separate tools and experiences. Workspace monitoring brings completed warehouse execution events into the WarehouseExecutions table, where administrators and operators can review activity across the workspace from a single monitoring database. The integration supports warehouses, SQL analytics endpoints, and warehouse snapshots. It captures completed, user-initiated queries that use distributed execution and records details such as duration, status, result codes, and CPU time. With this information in one place, you can spot failures or performance issues and focus your investigation on the affected warehouse and query.
